title: Release versions tag current valid premises
description: DECISION: Each Validatorium release references versioned assets and tags premises that are valid and current at that release. Eligibility checks versioned ontology terms, replacement UUID mappings, expiry/TTL, and recurrence. An ephemeral recurring premise can be current in each applicable window and inactive between windows without becoming obsolete; obsolescence is reserved for supersession.
close_reason: Recorded release-relative premise tagging, versioned artifact references, ontology remapping checks, and optional expiry/TTL evaluation in the data model.

title: Tag premises with versioned ontology terms
description: DECISION: Premises are tagged with versioned terms from versioned ontologies. A superseded term-mapping record is marked obsolete and stores reference pointers to its replacement record UUIDs; the obsolete record remains addressable through IPFS.
close_reason: Recorded the concise IPFS versioning rule in the ontology specifications.

title: Storage spike: embedded Kubo + go-orbit-db, two-node replication test

Test: node A writes a micropublication record, node B replicates it over pubsub; then partition and prove reconvergence. Success = two in-process nodes converge on the same record set. Directly attacks the go-orbit-db lag risk.

title: Publish additional attestations to the global store
description: The global pointer records one admitting attestation; there is no route for further attestations (other nodes, other methods) to reach the global store. distributed-datastore.md §8: 'A user may publish an attestation and its permitted evidence'.

title: Release and promotion: handle disagreeing attestations per the spec decision
description: release.pickAttestation and promote take one true attestation and ignore false ones, so a premise confirmed by one method and refuted by another is still released. Blocked on the spec decision for multiple methods.

title: Decide: spec rule for premises evaluated by multiple methods, including disagreement (fail bucket)
description:
data-model.md §1 core invariant: 'It is valid when its evaluation method returns true against its evidence and applicable context.' (singular). §6 allows any number of attestations, each with its own method, but no spec states the premise's status when attestations disagree (e.g. method A true, orthogonal method B false), and the fail bucket is not specified.

Owner direction 2026-11-16: the system must support any number of evaluations, methods and instances; anything in the spec that does not allow that must be fixed. Owner's earlier description of the fail bucket: claude.ai 'Initial greeting' 2026-07-14 msg 94.

Spec wording is the owner's decision; no spec text has been changed.

title: Evaluate a premise version with any registered method, not only its first method element (evaluate.Registry.Attest)
description: Attest selects the evaluator from the premise's first MP:Method element, so a second, orthogonal method cannot be run on the same premise version. Spec §6 attestations each name their method; allow the caller to name the method.
close_reason: evaluate.Registry.AttestWith evaluates a premise version with any registered method, including methods the premise record does not name; Attest delegates to it for the first-named method. val evaluate -method exposes it. Test: one premise version evaluated by two methods and repeated, each yielding its own attestation.

title: Wikipedia bulk ingestion: provisional validity for Wikipedia premises, batch-processed on Farscape
description:
Owner direction 2026-11-16 (verbatim): "we can basically download Wikipedia. It's 111 gigabytes. I can put it on this machine I have, which is called the Project Farscape. And we can process that using regular like commit. Like we can break it up into whatever structure we need, and we can run Validatorium and link all any premises that are in there using the ITVB based stuff, and we can basically have provisional valid for all of Wikipedia. Then we can run that like as a batch thing that's processing in the background using local agents."

Source facts (dumps.wikimedia.org/enwiki/latest, checked 2026-11-16): enwiki-latest-pages-articles.xml.bz2 25,899,045,155 bytes; pages-articles-multistream.xml.bz2 27,019,419,473 bytes (07-Nov-2026); pages-meta-current.xml.bz2 46,815,819,262 bytes. The multistream file has a separate index of independently decompressible bz2 streams, which permits parallel chunked processing. The 111 GB figure was not checked against a file listing.

Existing pieces this builds on: revision-pinned pointer records and equivalence re-check (internal/wikidata pattern: cite the source as a pointer, not as writ — validatorium-f47); evaluator registry (internal/evaluate); autopublish (internal/autopublish); ITVB self-certification registry (internal/api, validatorium-jkd).

Design points to settle: the record model has attestation results true/false/indeterminate; 'provisional valid' has no representation yet. A claim of the form 'enwiki revision R of page P states S' is checkable against the pinned revision bytes, as the wikidata-statement evaluator does for Wikidata.
notes:
2026-11-16 owner clarification (verbatim): "that's the flow, is that anyone can curate it. So if we say provisional, then it's curated, right? Using the normal process. I'm not changing anything about how I want to be clear. Validatorium has a very defined spec and it's very limited in scope. So, but I'm talking about feeding in stuff using an offline Wikipedia dump."

Correction to the description: no spec or record-model change. 'Provisional' is the existing candidate (draft) state in the working store; ingested premises enter there and go through the normal process (evaluation, promotion, obsoleting by anyone with agent and reason recorded). The 'design point' about a missing provisional status is withdrawn. Scope of this epic is the input feed from an offline Wikipedia dump only.

title: Self-certification registry (ITVB Seal of Truth) and verification HTTP API

HTTP API: GET /api/verification?url= answering in the ITVB response format, POST /api/certifications to register, POST /api/certifications/{uuid}/obsolete. Served by val api. GPG signature verification of the signer is a separate step (needs an OpenPGP dependency). Working branch only.

title: ITVB and IOA integration: browser plugin uses Validatorium; Validatorium cites ITVB/IOA records
description:
Integration of Validatorium with ITVB (Internet Truth Verification Board) and IOA, and their browser plugin. Relates to validatorium-bgk (truth.dataglut.org integration target).

Owner direction, 2026-11-16, verbatim:
- "I would point out ITVB uses this. The Internet Truth Verification Board uses this, so we would cite them, and they have a plugin for a browser, and it would use us."
- "and the IOA. So look up itvb.dataglut.org and ioa.dataglut.org. They use us and we use them."
- "And those repos either exist on GitHub or in Gitia. And the plugin is in, I think the IOA plugin, I think, is in the repo."
- "Or it might be in the Zuck stops here."
- "And if you have a working instance of a validatorium, then we could actually start using this almost immediately with the browser plugin."
- "The browser plugin could verify like IT, it could carry ITVB, right? Because ITVB is self-certifying, but the validatorium is a thing that holds premises, so a person could register in the validatorium, and it could have a class of like self-certified, because everything can be revoked, right, or obsoleted."
notes:
Owner direction, 2026-11-16, verbatim: "Revoke isn't right. Obsoleted would be the correct way. And so a person could self-obsolete, or anyone could obsolete it, right? Anything could be obsoleted, but all the records are tracked. So actually, we support ITVB as a registry for self-certification. And I guess the people who would self-certify would need to register certificates. So maybe we need to like basically have a mechanism for issue. If we could do like Let's Encrypt or GPG, yeah, we use GPG to register identity, like in the sense that Wikipedia has editors. You don't need to. You just use a GPG. If someone's untrustworthy, we revoke it." Then: "IOA is not the thing. Sorry, it's outrage.dataglut.org. And if you have access, yeah, it's linked from ITVB. So you need to do your fucking homework."
2026-11-16 findings: ITVB is the site at https://truth.dataglut.org ('International Truth Verification Board - Official Certification Authority'); it links to https://outrage.dataglut.org (Internet Outrage Authority, IOA; its classifications are 'independently verified by the ITVB'). Its Revocation section lists when a seal must be removed. Browser plugin: not found in the-zuck-stops-here, in GitHub search (no itvb/ioa repositories), or linked from either site. itvb.dataglut.org and ioa.dataglut.org resolve to 173.238.155.81 (the same host as Gitea) and reset connections from this cloud container.

title: Identity is attribution-only; GPG signing; anonymized; no klout
description: DECISION: identity tracked ONLY for attribution; premises stand on evidence alone. GPG signature from author's key attributes actions. Attribution anonymized (pseudonymous, not real-world identity). No klout/credit/reputation. PURPOSE: remediation — if an individual OR node corrupts data, enumerate & flag every record they touched. RATIONALE (owner). Supersedes agent-written did:key/Ed25519 self-gen scheme (unconfirmed).

title: Local vs global premises; sensitive/regional via compile-time cv tags
description: DECISION: local premises permitted only if they stay local AND do not conflict with any global premise on a matter of fact. 'sensitive' = public but content-flagged (e.g. not child-suitable). local/global/sensitive/regional handled by cv/ontology TAGS in record annotations + optional indices — not separate subsystems. All vocabularies/ontologies/cv-tables/data-structures FIXED AT COMPILE TIME, author-controlled. RATIONALE (owner).

title: Per-domain namespaced databases; UUID records + pointer namespaces
description: DECISION: per-domain DBs with owner-controlled namespaces (namespace:subdomain:...). Records are UUID-keyed; namespaces are a pointer layer — same premise may be referenced by multiple namespaced pointers. Core namespaces ship with the software (owner controls STRUCTURE, not truth). Private/shared namespaces ride on native IPFS mechanisms. RATIONALE (owner).

title: Automatic publication on validity
description: DECISION: software mechanically enforces validity rules; any NEW premise meeting minimum validity auto-publishes — no separate push step (the node runs IPFS, so local DB writing to the IPFS store IS replication). RATIONALE (owner). Accessibility invariant: a child can state a premise and see if it exists+valid or launch a validation task.
notes: 2026-11-16: implemented as internal/autopublish and val publish (branch claude/validatorium-implementation-td1o9u).

title: Leverage Micropublications ontology + semantic-web standards
description: DECISION: reuse the Micropublications OWL2 ontology (purl.org/mp, MIT) and lean on RDF/SPARQL and proper semantic-web standards throughout rather than reinventing. RATIONALE (owner): 'let's leverage as much proper semantic web standards as we can. SPARQL, RDF, etc.'

comments.author: brett
comments.text: OWNER (emphatic): USE THE MICROPUBLICATION ONTOLOGY (http://purl.org/mp). The model uses MP's claim/evidence/attribution structure; do NOT invent a parallel schema. Status vocabulary (validated/invalidated=proven/disproven, current/obsolete) grades over MP.

comments.author: brett
comments.text: MP model read from source (PMC4530550): a Claim is the principal truth-bearing Statement of a Micropublication. Grounding is STRUCTURAL, not a status label -- a Claim is grounded by a support-graph DAG rooted at the Claim; empirical evidence = Data (tables/images/measurements) + Method (reproducible recipe) + Material; minimal support = Attribution to an Agent. Dispute = challenges/hasChallengeGraphElement (structural). MP defines NO status/validity field.

comments.author: brett
comments.text: MP support vocabulary, verbatim from mp.owl (verified): dataSupports/supportedByData, evidenceSupports/supportedByEvidence, methodSupports/supportedByMethod, supports/supportedBy, hasSupportGraphElement/supportGraphElementOf; challenge side: challenges/challengedBy, hasChallengeGraphElement. 'refute' NOT present (not a science term). => evidence layer uses these MP properties; the invented 6-value evidence-type enum in data-model.md (empirical_observation/replication/model_prediction/historical_record/civil_record/expert_testimony) is software-invented and to be replaced with MP (Data/Method/Material) -- and, if finer evidence typing is wanted, the ECO standard (verify, do not assert).

title: Micropublication core model + full lexical grounding
description: DECISION: record = statement + validity grade + supporting citations, each with own UUID/accession/ontology annotation; no arguments/talk-pages/social layer in the record. EVERY word in the statement grounded to a domain jargon dictionary/ontology OR standard language definition (stricter than data-model.md). Software proposes annotation+provenance under human curation. RATIONALE (owner): micropublications model; 'if someone did all that work already, we should implement it.'

comments.author: brett
comments.text: OWNER (verbatim): "Each premise by definition must have a 'minimal string representation' that serves as the statement of the premise; eg: 'sky is blue'". => The premise's statement IS its minimal string representation — the canonical shortest form. This is the 'shorthand / short string' referenced by the text-generation feature (validatorium-3xe).

comments.author: brett
comments.text: OWNER correctness point: '\''apples are red'\'' is NOT a true premise (universal reading, false — overgeneralization the scope rules reject). The valid minimal form is '\''apples can be red'\''. => The minimal string representation must be the shortest form that is STILL a valid premise; brevity must not cost correctness. Good: '\''sky is blue'\'', '\''apples can be red'\''. Invalid: '\''apples are red'\''.

comments.author: brett
comments.text: Shorthand note (owner) -- do not over-engineer: the minimal string representation could be encoded efficiently using formal-logic symbols. Recorded as a possibility; not a blocker, not to be fixated on.

comments.author: brett
comments.text: IMPLEMENTED: internal/model/model.go — micropublication record built from docs/specs/mp.owl. Every field maps to an MP class/property (documented in comments): Claim=MP:Claim (principal Statement), statement text=MP:statement (the minimal string), evidence=MP:Data/Method/Material via supportedByData/Method/Evidence collected in a support graph (MP:hasSupportGraphElement), challenge graph=MP:hasChallengeGraphElement, citations=MP:Reference/citation, term grounding=MP:SemanticQualifier/semtags, attribution=MP:Attribution/attributedTo/atTime. NO validated/invalidated status (system stores only valid premises). UUID identity + current/obsolete versioning flagged as project layer (MP has neither). Serializes to the _id-keyed go-orbit-db Documents map the spike uses. gofmt/vet clean; 4 tests pass (New/UUID-uniqueness/admission-gate/document-round-trip); whole repo builds.

title: Integrations & standards
description: Leverage existing standards/systems: Micropublications OWL2 ontology (purl.org/mp); microPublication Biology journal conventions (CRediT roles, DOIs, structured metadata); Wikidata/SPARQL for term grounding; truth.dataglut.org integration (Schema.org JSON-LD + HTTP API — owner: real integration target). Prefer RDF/SPARQL/semantic-web standards throughout.

title: Identity, signing & accountability
description: Identity tracked ONLY for attribution — premises stand on evidence alone; identity carries no validity weight. GPG signature from author's key attributes actions (authored premise / attached evidence / flagged claim). Attribution is anonymized (consistent pseudonymous signer, not real-world identity). No klout/credit/reputation/leaderboards. PURPOSE: remediation — if an individual OR node is found corrupting data, enumerate & flag every record they touched. Minimal OpenID login for PORTABLE preferences/config stored in the distributed DB (login from any instance; age-gates sensitive content).

title: Namespaces & governance
description: Per-domain databases with owner-controlled namespaces (form namespace:subdomain:...). UUID-keyed records; namespaces are a POINTER layer (one record may be referenced by multiple namespaced pointers). Core validatorium namespaces ship with the software (author/engineer controls STRUCTURE, not truth). Users add private/shared namespaces (ride on native IPFS mechanisms). Local vs global premises (local must stay local + not conflict with global on fact). Sensitive/regional handled via cv/ontology tags in record annotations + optional indices. All vocabularies/ontologies/cv-tables/structures fixed at COMPILE time.

title: Validation & epistemic-grading engine
description: Mechanical, evidence-based validity determination. Truth determined by evidence alone, universally, zero exceptions — no special/protected/axiomatic premises. Software enforces validity rules; a new premise meeting minimum validity auto-publishes. Accessibility invariant: a child can run the software, state a premise, see whether it already exists+valid, or launch a validation task.

comments.author: brett
comments.text: CORE INVARIANT (owner, emphatic, verbatim): 'ALL PREMISES MUST BE VALID IN THE SYSTEM' / 'THE SYSTEM ONLY STORES VALID PREMISES.' Validity is the admission gate -- invalid candidates are rejected and never stored; there is no stored-invalid-premise state. Ex: 'apples are red' rejected (overgeneralized); 'apples can be red' admitted.

comments.author: brett
comments.text: PREMISE STATUS VOCABULARY (owner): a factual premise is VALIDATED / INVALIDATED (i.e. PROVEN / DISPROVEN by evidence) and CURRENT / OBSOLETE. Facts are proven or disproven, never 'contradicted', never argued. The agent-invented 5-value epistemic enum + argument-based status word are purged from all docs (data-model.md, README.md, evidence-verification.md, participation-model.md, premise-decomposition.md) and replaced by these two axes.

comments.author: brett
comments.text: CONSEQUENCE from MP source: MP has NO status field. 'Proven vs disproven' is represented as presence of supporting vs challenging empirical evidence in the support graph, not a stored word. The validated/invalidated prose in the docs is therefore software-composed/provisional, not MP-grounded, and must be reconciled to MP structure. CURRENT/OBSOLETE = versioning (IPFS layer), not MP.

title: Micropublication data model (RDF-grounded)
description: Core record = a micropublication: (1) statement — one short atomic factual claim; (2) validity grade; (3) supporting citations to empirical evidence. Each object carries its own UUID/accession + ontology annotation. Identity = UUID assigned at creation (NOT content-hash); statement text may be refined under same ID; premises may split (obsolete+redirect) or be obsoleted. Every word in the statement is grounded to a domain jargon dictionary/ontology OR standard language definitions (stricter than agent-written data-model.md). Leverage the Micropublications OWL2 ontology (purl.org/mp, MIT) and semantic-web standards (RDF/SPARQL) rather than reinventing.

title: Use-case walkthrough flags: Jeff's favorite food (compare notes before any spec change)
description:
Running list of gaps the agent flagged while walking through the Jeff use case with the owner. Flags only: no spec changes until the owner compares notes and decides.

Spec gaps:
F1. A person's own statement about themselves is not an evidence type (evidence-verification.md table lists measurement, published study, dataset, public record, artifact, computation, runtime observation, instrument output).
F2. Self-referential premises (author, subject and evidence source are the same key) are not defined.
F3. No rule for how a syncing node treats a set of self-referential premises.

Code gaps (spec already supports):
F4. Premise model lacks the spec's terms field (TermGrounding).
F5. Premise model lacks the spec's temporal_policy field; only attestation expiry is implemented.
F6. No decomposition tool (premise-decomposition.md).
F7. No derivation step for derived premises (e.g. outer expiry from a longevity bound, anti-premises).
F8. Private namespaces not implemented; publishing requires a true attestation.
notes:
Protocol (owner, 2026-11-16): owner-raised items are logged here too, each with the agent's spec check (section + quote, or 'not covered'). Every agent assessment, including 'covered', is provisional until owner and agent check it together. No spec changes during the walkthrough.
F9 (owner-raised, agent spec check): 'yes, and' interaction. The system accepts the user's statement without rejecting or correcting it, assumes nothing about the user's background, walks back to the root premise ('who are you?' 'Jeff'), then proceeds one premise at a time in the user's own words ('and what's next?'). Agent spec check (provisional): structural steps covered by participation-model.md §3 'Ambiguity processing is structural' (identify, ground, refine or decompose, evaluate each atomic premise); the interaction itself is not covered by any spec.
F9 addendum (owner): the 'yes, and' flow is a graph traversal starting from what can be established from the statement. Agent spec check (provisional): premise-decomposition.md §4 defines decomposition as recursive descent to terminal premises ('Keep decomposing until you reach claims that can ONLY be verified by direct observation or direct reference to definitions'); traversal order for the interaction is not specified.
F10 (agent-raised, needs joint check): premise-decomposition.md §4 termination criteria say stop when 'Further decomposition would manufacture philosophical claims about existence rather than identify genuinely independent verifiable facts (see Section 6)'. The Jeff walkthrough roots on an existence premise ('there is a person named Jeff'). Agent provisional reading: legitimate, because it concerns a particular checkable entity (this key holder, named Jeff), not existence in the abstract. To be confirmed together.
F11 (owner-raised, agent spec check): term mapping comes from the person making the premise; when a term has two or more candidate mappings, the system presents them to the person at that step ('is it this or that?'). The system is a formal mapping system, not AI-based. Agent spec check (provisional): covered in part. llm-integration.md failure table: 'Ontology Grounding | Ambiguous match (multiple QIDs) | Human for disambiguation'; 'A person may ... resolve ambiguous grounding'; data-model.md §4 TermGrounding keeps surface_form (the person's word) with the mapping; llm-integration.md: 'THE LLM PROPOSES. EVIDENCE EVALUATION DETERMINES VALIDITY.' Open: (a) spec says 'may', not 'must', and does not say whether unambiguous automatic mappings need the author's confirmation; (b) human disambiguation is specified only inside the LLM pipeline, not for a formal non-LLM lookup path.
F11 clarification (owner): the disambiguation is visual, not a question dialog. The decomposed premise is shown with its terms marked; each term with more than one candidate mapping has a drop-down of the candidates, and the person picks the correct one. Agent spec check (provisional): not covered. No spec describes a user interface for term mapping (no drop-down, term highlighting or visual mapping selection in docs/specs). Related open epic: validatorium-dq2 (Web UI).
F12 (owner-raised, agent spec check): overloaded premises. A person may mean two things at once, both true; overloading is not necessarily either/or. Agent spec check (provisional): covered by decomposition. participation-model.md §3 'Refine or decompose the candidate'; premise-decomposition.md §3.1 splits conjunctions; each reading becomes its own atomic premise with its own mapping, evaluated independently; one premise cannot carry two meanings (one evaluable assertion per premise). Not covered: the visual mapping step must allow selecting more than one mapping, splitting the premise per selected reading, rather than forcing a single choice (interface unspecified; see F11).
Scenario (owner, constructed): Jeff is gay; Jeff likes strawberry Pop-Tarts; gay men statistically prefer strawberry Pop-Tarts; Jeff likes them because he likes them, not because he is gay; a hypothetical gene linkage could make the causal link provable; the system suggests 'you might be gay' and Jeff confirms. Owner point: the system contains its own validity and surfaces it; only valid things are in it. Agent spec check (provisional): covered, data-model.md §1 'Only valid premises enter the validated premise store.'
F13 (agent, covered, provisional): a causal 'because' about an individual needs its own premises; population statistics do not establish it. premise-decomposition.md §3.2: 'The causal link between Y and X is itself a claim that may need its own premises.' Inference outputs are conclusions, not premises (§3.3).
F14 (agent, not covered): the system proposing to a person a conclusion about that person inferred from population premises (e.g. 'you might be gay'). Not specified: whether the system surfaces inferences about individuals; base-rate handling (P(A|B) is not P(B|A)); treatment of sensitive personal attributes such as sexual orientation. The privacy invariant (llm-integration.md 'No data leaves the local machine. Ever.') covers data movement, not inference. A person's confirmation records a new self-referential premise; it does not validate the inference.
STEP 0, identity and personhood (owner, 2026-11-16). Correction: the speaker identifies as himself ('My name's Jeff, and I like, my favorite food is...'); the root is the speaker (first person), and 'my name is Jeff' is one premise about him. Agent breakdown wrongly made 'there is a person named Jeff' the root.
F15 (owner): before anything else the system establishes a formal entity, a person, who is the speaker; everything entered is then self-referential. Some self-referential premises are independently verifiable by others (someone could watch Jeff eat Pop-Tarts). Spec check (provisional): not covered; no person/self entity is defined; F1-F2 apply.
F16 (owner): no official curators. Anyone may curate (fictional example: 'Friends of Project X' / 'Curators Guild of Project X', unofficial). Spec check (provisional): covered. participation-model.md §4 'What Does Not Exist': 'Editorial authority over factual validity'.
F17 (owner): informed consent at the first step: the system is swarm-based and potentially a global registry; self-referential information can be synced into the world. Spec check (provisional): partial. distributed-datastore.md §9 'Require user authorization for publication and local observation'; §8 local by default. No consent notice about global replication is specified.
F18 (owner): the person is the authority over their self-referential premises and related premises: can control and recall (obsolete) them; premises others make about the person raise revocation questions handled through certificates. Spec check (provisional): not covered. Obsolete lifecycle exists; subject authority over premises about them is not specified.
F19 (owner): a person's existence is not within their legal control; users acknowledge the laws of their jurisdiction and international law (two-way requirement); the system respects and supports compliance mechanisms but does not actively enforce. Spec check (provisional): not covered; no spec addresses legal compliance or jurisdiction.
F20 (owner): obsoleted records remain in the system but are not exposed, potentially encrypted; all data can be encrypted; the system is closed against tampering and anonymized by definition; legally withdrawn data can disappear from exposure instantly while remaining in the system. Spec check (provisional): not covered (no encryption, erasure or tamper-resistance spec). Tension to check together: data-model.md §4 says obsolete records 'remain addressable through IPFS'; content-addressed blocks replicated to other peers cannot be recalled from those peers. Known technique matching 'potentially encrypted': per-record encryption with key destruction ('crypto-shredding'), which makes replicated ciphertext unreadable. Relevant law example: GDPR Article 17 (right to erasure).
Context (owner, not a spec item): the operating entity is EPNI Global, a Swiss Verein whose single mission is pro-social promotion of freedom and technology in the public good; non-political except pro-humanity: do not hurt people, promote science and human advancement, non-tribal; 'Human advancement without intervention. The Star Trek model.'
Context (owner, verbatim): 'We don't take sides in a war. We take all sides.'
Correction to F4: the premise model does have term groundings, under Statement.Terms (internal/model/model.go: SurfaceForm, OntologyURI, Sense). F4 is withdrawn; only the temporal_policy part (F5) stands.
Live run of the walkthrough on the owner's own statements (2026-11-16): Erdős number 4 (supported: PubMed PMID 18404212 co-authored with J. Craig Venter, listed with Erdős number 3); sister Dr. Carolyn Whitty at CAMH (supported by primary source: CPSO register #88876, primary business location and hospital privileges CAMH); cousins in Superman II (indeterminate, recorded); sister in the Crash Test Dummies video (indeterminate; she is the authority, F18). Agent error: questioned before accepting and used secondary sources first, the opposite of the 'yes, and' step.
Spec checks (agent, provisional): absence of evidence gives indeterminate, not false: covered (attestation results true|false|indeterminate; participation-model.md §4 lists 'An unsupported premise state in the validated store' under What Does Not Exist). Registry lookups as evidence: covered (evidence-verification.md: 'Public record', 'Dataset or database record').
F21 (owner, not covered): evaluation should go to the authoritative primary source for the kind of premise first (e.g. the regulator's register for a physician), before any secondary source; no spec states source precedence.
F22 (owner-raised, agent spec check): premise and anti-premise relationships revealed through the structure and queryable through ontologies. Agent check (provisional): not covered. No spec mentions negation, anti-premises, disjointness or complement. Implemented today: support/challenge graphs (MP supports/challenges), term groundings as URIs, dependency links. Not implemented: an anti-premise relation, derivation from ontology axioms, any ontology store or query layer (groundings are bare URIs; no reasoner or SPARQL). The repo's Micropublications ontology (docs/specs/mp.owl v1.18) has supports, challenges, directly/indirectlyChallenges, qualifiedBy, curatedBy, but no negation or disjointness between statements. Sources of such relations: OWL vocabulary (owl:disjointWith, owl:complementOf, owl:AllDisjointClasses, owl:NegativePropertyAssertion); Wikidata properties P461 'opposite of' and P1889 'different from'. Only Wikidata term records (internal/wikidata) are drawn on today.
F23 (owner-raised, agent spec check): asynchronous curation workers. Agent check (provisional): not covered. No spec text mentions curation, curators or curation workers. Related existing pieces: data-model.md §11 'An authorized orchestrator may execute a method'; model.Attribution.Curator field; MP attributionAsCurator and curatedBy properties.

title: Premise clusters: every equivalent statement of a premise (paraphrase + cross-language)
description:
DECISION (owner): The software GENERATES 'premise clusters'.

DEFINITION (owner, verbatim): "A 'premise cluster' is basically every possible version of stating the same premise (and if we support languages other than English, in every possible language the premise can be stated in)."
=> A cluster = all equivalent human-readable statements of the SAME premise: minimal string representation, formal-logic-encoded form, paraphrases/restatements, and (if multilingual) translations.

ANCHOR (owner, verbatim): "The UUID is the only string you AS SOFTWARE need to concern your ... head about" and "Short strings are for HUMANS."
=> One premise = one UUID = one cluster of equivalent strings. The software addresses premises by UUID only (identity, keys, references, pointers); it never parses a string to determine identity. The short strings are HUMAN-facing surface forms held in the cluster. Refining/adding a statement adds a cluster member without changing the UUID.

title: Decide: sort the OrbitDB write-access list when a global store opens
description:
**Decision needed:** Whether the go-orbit-db global store sorts its write-access identity list when it opens.

**Provenance:** `internal/orbit/orbit.go` (Options.WriteAccess), `internal/orbit/namespace.go`; commit d036bdc; relates to validatorium-bqe.6. Reported in prose on 2026-11-05 and not asked as a question. Raised 2026-11-12 by the validatorium cloud session, actor gemini-cli.

**What I already checked:** Vendored go-orbit-db source: a store address is the hash of its manifest (name, type, access-controller address), and the access-controller address derives from the write list as given. `internal/orbit/namespace_test.go` asserts that same-order lists converge on two nodes. docs/specs: no rule on write-list order. `docs/design/two-tier-storage.md` section 6 lists access control as an item to revisit.

**Situation (facts only):** Two peers that pass the same identities in a different order compute different store addresses and do not replicate. Sorting at open removes that. Sorting changes the address of any store already created from an unsorted list of more than one identity. This session knows of no such store outside tests.

**Pre-answered:** Does a single-identity list change? No. Is there a deployed multi-writer store? None known to this session.

**Gates:** Nothing now. Needed before a multi-writer deployment.

title: Text generation engine: local model (gemma4) drafts prose from premises + glue text
description:
OWNER (verbatim): "a 'text generation engine' that uses a local model like gemma4 to author draft text based on the premises (and perhaps user-authored glue text as well); the premises could be added using their 'shorthand' / 'short string' representations."

=> Local LLM (gemma4 via Ollama) generates DRAFT text from a set of premises, optionally with user-authored 'glue' text. Premises inserted via their shorthand = the minimal string representation that IS each premise's statement (validatorium-8gv). LLM drafts; human authors/curates.

comments.author: brett
comments.text: RESOLVED (owner): the shorthand/short-string representation = the premise's 'minimal string representation', which by definition serves as the statement of the premise (e.g. 'sky is blue'). Defined at the data-model level — see validatorium-8gv. No separate syntax to design.

title: Argument builder: search premises -> toolkit -> construct arguments (kid-friendly)
description:
OWNER (verbatim): "for kids, they could play with an 'argument builder' where they search for premises, add them to a 'toolkit', and then use the toolkit to construct arguments."

=> Interactive tool: search premises, collect chosen ones into a per-user 'toolkit', then assemble them into arguments. Kid-friendly framing (ties to the accessibility principle: a child can use the system). Product layer; composes with the README 'premises compose into larger arguments' vision and the Argdown module.

title: cytoscape.js graph view of a premise + supporting evidence types
description:
OWNER (verbatim): "a cytoscape.js graphical representation would be perfect for viewing an individual premise, and the supporting evidence types."

=> Render a single premise as a cytoscape.js graph: the premise plus its supporting evidence, distinguished by evidence type (per the micropublication model's evidence types).

title: Web UI: browse/search Validatorium + graphical premise exploration
description:
OWNER (verbatim): "In a polished finished product, users could explore a web view of the 'Validatorium', search for premises; a cytoscape.js graphical representation would be perfect for viewing an individual premise, and the supporting evidence types."

=> Web exploration surface for a finished product: browse/search premises + a cytoscape.js graph of a premise and its supporting evidence types. Future/product layer, in addition to the Go CLI primary interface (README).
